analysis.one_liner: Phases out federal sugar price supports, loans, and import quotas.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote; it was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in January 2011 and died there when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law keeps U.S. sugar prices above world levels through government-backed loans to sugar processors, a price support program, and limits on how much sugar can be imported. This bill would phase those supports down to zero by the 2015 crop, end the marketing quotas that restrict supply, and direct the Agriculture Department to raise the tariff-rate quotas on imported sugar so American sugar prices fall closer to world levels. The bill was never taken up by the Senate Agriculture Committee and never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who pay higher grocery prices for sugar-sweetened foods under the current program, and food and candy manufacturers, who buy sugar as an input. Independent analyses of the sugar program have found U.S. sugar prices run roughly double world market prices, costing consumers and food-using businesses billions of dollars a year, with a small group of growers and processors capturing the benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Phases the sugar loan rate down each year from 2012 through 2014 until it reaches $0 for the 2015 crop, ending federal price support loans for sugarcane and sugar beet processors [S2, S3].
Repeals the sugar marketing quotas and allotments that restrict how much sugar can be grown and sold domestically [S2, S3].
Directs the Secretary of Agriculture to increase the tariff-rate quotas on imported raw and refined sugar to ensure an adequate supply of sugar at reasonable prices in the United States [S2, S3].
Ends related subsidies, including forfeited-sugar storage payments, sugar processor storage facility loans, and the feedstock flexibility program for bioenergy producers [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sugarcane and sugar beet growers and sugar processors, who would lose guaranteed above-market prices, government loans, and protection from import competition. Growers in beet-producing states would face the most abrupt adjustment after the phase-down window ends.

drawbacks.text: Ending price supports and marketing quotas would expose sugar growers to world market price swings with little protection, and growers argue the U.S. program supports domestic production that would otherwise move offshore, raising reliance on foreign suppliers [S2].

The bill phases out supports over four years but then eliminates all price support, processor loans, and marketing quotas at once beginning with the 2015 crop, an abrupt endpoint that would be difficult for sugar beet farmers in producing states [S2, S3].

The bill still directs the Secretary to ensure 'a robust and competitive sugar processing industry in the United States' when raising import quotas, so it moderates rather than fully frees sugar trade [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is broad and diffuse: roughly every household that buys sweetened food pays a hidden premium for sugar under the current program, and this bill would gradually eliminate that premium while giving growers a four-year adjustment window. The cost falls on a small, geographically concentrated group of growers and processors who currently receive guaranteed above-market prices with no cost to taxpayers when loans are repaid at supported prices. The main honest objection is adjustment risk to beet farmers and exposure to volatile world prices, which the four-year phase-down partially but not fully addresses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen introduced the bill on January 25, 2011, with Sens. Mark Kirk and Richard Durbin as original cosponsors [S1, S3].
Ten senators — 7 Republicans and 3 Democrats — cosponsored the bill [S4].

The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry on January 25, 2011; the action history shows no committee markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The 112th Congress ended January 3, 2013, with the bill still sitting in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar growers and processors are better off because the bill died: the federal price support program, government-backed loans, and import quotas that keep U.S. sugar prices above world levels all remained in place, and consumers continued paying the resulting premium at the grocery store.

for.name: Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to phase out the federal sugar program.

against.name: Debbie Stabenow
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: The committee never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress; it remained referred there until the Congress ended.

against.name: American Sugar Alliance
against.role: Trade association of U.S. sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors
against.what_they_did: Actively opposed reform of the federal sugar program, including efforts like this bill, through lobbying and member-state pressure.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan and slightly tilted Republican: of the bill's 10 cosponsors, 7 were Republicans and 3 were Democrats, and the bill itself was never voted on by either party's leadership.

industries.industry: Sugar growers and processors (sugarcane and sugar beet)
industries.note: The current program guarantees them above-market prices through government loans, price supports, and import quotas; this bill would phase all of it out. Their benefit under the status quo comes directly from higher sugar prices paid by consumers and food companies.

They buy sugar as a major input, so ending the program and raising import quotas would lower their largest ingredient cost, savings that would partly reach consumers. Several major food companies have publicly pushed for exactly this reform.
Higher tariff-rate quotas would let them sell more sugar into the U.S. market at competitive prices, which is what brings U.S. prices down for consumers.
